What the bill actually bans is $CRCL or any issuer paying users savings-account-like interest just for holding USDC. What it preserves is rewards tied to activity(caveat imo): trading, transactions, staking on a platform like $COIN. $COIN commands 50% of USDC revenue through its equity stake in $CRCL , and uses part of that share to fund the activity-based rewards that incentivize usage.

To all the @elonmusk fans and @Starlink $TSLA  fans - I respect what @SpaceX has built. But let me show you why Starlink Mobile isn't even playing the same game as $ASTS , and why ASTS is trading at a steal right now.
It comes down to spectrum. And once you understand spectrum, the entire D2D picture becomes obvious.
Think of radio spectrum like sound from a speaker. Bass notes are low frequency - they travel far, go through walls, you feel them in the next room. 
Treble notes are high frequency - crisp and clear but step behind a wall and they disappear. This is physics. Can't be engineered around no matter how many satellites you launch. 

Here's who owns what in D2D:

LOW-BAND - the bass. Goes through walls, buildings, cars.
→ 700 MHz: AT&T and FirstNet own it. Leased to ASTS. FCC authorized for 248 satellites. This reaches you inside your house, in a basement, in a parking garage.
→ 800/850 MHz: AT&T and Verizon own it. Leased to ASTS. FCC authorized. Same indoor penetration.
→ 902-928 MHz: Federal radiolocation band. ASTS filed to test radar here for the Space Force starting June 12. Defense revenue on a different frequency.
Nobody else has D2D authorization on low-band. Not SpaceX. Not Amazon. Not Qualcomm. It's all owned by carriers who spent tens of billions at auctions over decades to lock it up.

MID-BAND — the treble. Outdoor only. Does not penetrate buildings.
→ SpaceX: ~65 MHz owned (AWS-3, AWS-4, H-Block, 1695-2180 MHz range). Paid $17B+ for it through EchoStar. Real spectrum. But current phones don't support these bands. SpaceX's own VP said commercial launch mid-2027. And even then mid-band still doesn't go indoors.
→ SpaceX current D2D: T-Mobile PCS (~1900 MHz), leased. Powers Starlink Mobile today at 3-7 Mbps. Texting and basic data. Outdoors only. T-Mobile CEO said they're seeing "a lot less usage than originally thinking."
→ Amazon/Globalstar: ~25 MHz total. 8 MHz L-band + 16.5 MHz S-band. Asymmetric — caps two-way throughput. Narrowband, not broadband. D2D system not launching until 2028 at earliest. Amazon paid $11.6B for this.
→ Ligado: 45 MHz L-band. FCC approval pending for 7+ years. GPS lobby blocking it.

Tokenized stocks are now a working market on-chain, you can trade equities like $TSLA, $NVDA, $AAPL directly on crypto rails.

What matters most is the legal structure behind each token🧵 👇

There are four major tokenized stock systems shaping this space right now:

→ Backpack Securities ($SPCX)
→ Ondo Global Markets
→ xStocks (Backed Finance)
→ PreStocks
All of them track stocks, none of them represent the same legal rights.

◢  $SPCX by @Backpack Securities sits closest to real equity ownership. It is backed 1:1 with actual shares held in regulated custody. 

Qualified users can redeem tokens into real shares through traditional settlement systems like ACATS/DTCC.

That creates a direct path into real-world ownership.

Once redeemed, holders gain standard equity rights:
 • dividends
• corporate actions
• transfer rights

But on-chain tokens themselves still sit inside an SPV structure until redemption happens.

◢ $Ondo Global Markets uses a structured note model that each token is backed by real securities plus additional collateral.

The structure is designed around bankruptcy-remote SPVs, independent trustees, and continuous verification.

The system is built for financial stability and transparency, but holders do not become shareholders.

There are no voting rights, no ownership claims, and no direct equity status.
The product is engineered exposure, not equity transfer.

◢ @xStocksFi by @BackedFi is designed for DeFi trading because it integrates directly into protocols like @jup_dao, @Raydium, and @kamino.

It allows 24/7 trading of stock exposure inside crypto markets, however, it does not transfer shareholder rights.

Users hold price exposure only. Dividends, voting rights, and legal ownership are not part of the structure.

In some cases, backing may include cash or alternative collateral rather than direct stock custody.

◢ @PreStocks operates in private-market exposure, it tracks companies such as @OpenAI, @AnthropicAI, and @SpaceX before IPO.

The structure is the weakest in terms of enforceable ownership.

There are no shareholder rights at all: 
• no voting
• no dividends
• no legal ownership
• no information rights

Only synthetic exposure through SPVs.
In May 2026, disputes around share transfer validity triggered sharp price drops of 34–40% in affected tokens.

That event exposed the legal fragility of synthetic private exposure when underlying agreements are challenged.

Across all these systems, one important reality exists “There are two parallel price systems” which are:

• on-chain trading price (crypto markets, 24/7)
• underlying stock price (traditional markets)

Arbitrage keeps them aligned when liquidity exists, when it does not exist, gaps form and these gaps appear during weekends, low liquidity periods, and in private-market tokens.

Most trading activity is concentrated in a small set of liquid names like $TSLAx, $NVDAx, $CRCLx, $SPCX, and more 

Regulators now classify tokenized stocks into three categories:

• ownership-linked instruments
• custodial receipt models
• synthetic exposure products

Each category carries different legal rights, even when the price charts look identical.

What this market is building is not just “crypto versions of stocks.” It is a split system of financial design:

» Some tokens connect to real equity ownership.
» Some are structured financial notes with collateral.
» Some are pure synthetic exposure to price movement.

→ The key point is simple:

The ticker is not the asset but the legal structure behind the token is the asset.
That is what defines what you actually hold.

1. Auto Margins ex Credits: I expect auto gross margin ex-credits to be slightly above the Street's 18.5% because volumes were so strong. It was 19.2% in March. In theory, it should be flat quarter over quarter.

2. Deliveries: Key question is what drove the surge in June deliveries, up 25% y/y compared to up 6% in March? I believe high gas prices is a sustainable tailwind.

3. Capex. Here’s the negative wildcard. Last quarter, when the company guided capex to increase this year from $20B to $25B, it triggered a sell-off in after-hours trading, underscoring that the topic matters. I expect the company to guide to a number above $25B this year and give hints that 2027 should be above the Street’s $21B level.

4. Robotaxi. In July they added 3 cities and now operate small fleets in 7 cities. They’ve said two more cities coming, Las Vegas and Phoenix. I expect 3 more by year end, getting us to 10 in total. Street is expecting 2-3 more this year.

5. FSD. In March active paid subs grew 51% YY to 1.28m. In June I expect growth of 40%. The strong June delivery number should result in an acceleration in active sub growth in September because sales in the US come with one month free that acts as a top of funnel. FSD is approved in the Netherlands (April) and waiting for approval in the EU and China.

6. Cybercab: I expect Elon to move the target for production ramp from late 2026 to first half of 2027. My take: Investors are already expecting the slip.

7. Optimus. I’m not expecting much substance. Long term, 2040, this should be more than half of sales.

Toy department: SpaceX acquiring Tesla: We won’t get anything tonight on the topic. I put the odds at 80% that Tesla will be acquired by SpaceX within the next five years.

The idea that $TSLA ATH is some kind of hard floor for any acquisition, and that shareholders would “never” approve a deal below it, is just flat-out wrong.

Real completed deals prove it:

• Microsoft bought Activision Blizzard for $95/share. Its ATH was around $104. The deal closed below ATH.

• Elon bought Twitter for $54.20/share. Its ATH was $77.63. The deal closed far below ATH.

This happens all the time. Acquisition premiums are paid over the current unaffected share price, not over some previous ATH. Boards and shareholders regularly approve deals below ATH when the offer is attractive relative to where the stock is trading, the company’s standalone prospects, execution risk and the available alternatives.

The same logic applies to any potential SpaceX-Tesla deal. A low TSLA share price does not magically create some unbreakable ATH floor. It also does not automatically mean Tesla is “cheap” in absolute dollar terms.

The real questions are valuation, exchange ratio, strategic value, governance and what shareholders are getting versus the alternatives.

Pretending old $TSLA ATH is sacred, untouchable or economically decisive is pure nonsense. It is just anchoring bias dressed up as corporate finance.

These AV risks are also mainly offset thanks to Uber's pretty large partner network such as: Lucid-Nuro (SF), Zoox (Vegas), Wayve (London/Tokyo) and WeRide (Europe).

(Uber is around 7-8 turns below the growth adjusted multiple vs. peers...crazy).

There were also recent reports that Waymo are planning to end their arrangement with Uber in Atlanta/Austin after the term ends in Jan'28. 

I think that getting rid of Waymo is good for Uber...not bad as many believe because it gives Uber additional wiggle room for U.S. expansion by using a broader partner network. 

Even without Waymo, Uber is in a strong place to win in autonomous vehicles. They've grown their partnerships in the U.S. at quite an impressive rate in the U.S. alone (I think over 8+ in total), which means they're relatively self-sufficent if any one partner comes under risk. Plus, plans are in place to scale from 7 -> 15 cities with AVs by

Many people will still want a human to drive them places, not a robot.

Is Merger Uncertainty Holding Back $TSLA and $SPCX?

Is the market just waiting on a $TSLA / $SPCX deal — and parking both stocks until somebody says the quiet part out loud?

Short answer: yes, uncertainty is sitting on both names. Longer answer: it is not the whole story.

What we actually know:

No merger has been announced. No S-4. No exchange ratio.

What we do have is Elon leaving the door wide open. “Who can imagine what action one might take when there’s so much close collaboration.” On the Tesla earnings call it was the same idea: more and more overlap, but any merger or acquisition has to go through the appropriate process.

Some analysts have been throwing around 80% to 90% odds of a combination over the next year or two. Prediction markets have been a lot more conservative on pricing a 2026 announcement. Both can be true at the same time. High conviction that it happens eventually is not the same thing as high conviction that it happens next month.

This morning there was another small governance wrinkle: Tesla making it easier for retail to set standing voting instructions. That kind of change matters if a Tesla shareholder vote is ever required. SpaceXAI does not need one. Elon already controls that board. The stocks barely cared. $SPCX was a little green. $TSLA was red. That tells you the market is treating M&A as a medium-term possibility, not an imminent catalyst.

Where price actually is:

As of this morning, $SPCX is hanging around $149–$150. IPO was $135 on June 12. It ran toward $225, then gave most of that back. Still above the IPO price. Roughly a $2 trillion company.

$TSLA is in the high $340s to low $350s, off a 52-week high near $499. Call it a $1.4 trillion company. Down on the day while SpaceXAI is not.

That relative gap has widened since the IPO. That matters, because it changes the math of who is buying whom and how many new $SPCX shares get printed to do it.

If a deal happens, I expect it is more likely $SPCX acquires $TSLA than the other way around. So Tesla holders should be thinking in terms of a premium. And SpaceXAI holders should be thinking in terms of dilution. Those two facts can send the stocks in opposite directions even before anything is official.

Why “both stocks are suppressed by merger talk” is only half right:

Merger uncertainty is a real overhang.

$TSLA holders do not know if they get a premium, become a substitute index for SpaceX, or get absorbed into a vehicle Elon already votes. Some capital will sit on its hands until the terms are knowable.

$SPCX holders do not know how many shares they will issue, whether they inherit Tesla’s China exposure and auto cyclicality, or whether they are using an expensive stock as cheap currency. Lockup supply is already a problem. A giant stock deal on top of that is another problem.

If the market decides a merger is “next and soon,” $TSLA can start trading more like a SpaceX tracking stock instead of an auto-and-energy company. That is a real risk to price discovery.

So yes. The lack of a clean yes or no is keeping some buyers on the sidelines.

Tesla is still being graded on deliveries, margins, and how much it is spending to get to robotaxi, Cybercab, and Optimus. Delivery weeks have been sell-the-news events even when the print looks fine. Gross margin has been compressed. Capex is heavy. Cybercab is under regulator questions. The multiple is still extreme. That is a standalone story.

SpaceXAI has its own tape. Tiny float at the IPO. Staggered lockups dumping more supply into the market. Heavy AI spend after folding in xAI. Starship costs. A big bond raise. Insider selling. That combination explains the fade from $225 better than “maybe they buy TSLA instead of SPCX.”

$SPCX popped, unwound, and price is still currently above the IPO. That makes sense as post-IPO digestion plus float.

(Continued) 🧵

The part that does keep a lid on both:

The deal structure is messy, and messy structure is what markets hate.

If SpaceX is the buyer, the exchange ratio is the whole game.

A modest premium can look like a gift to $TSLA holders and an insult to $SPCX holders at the same time. A large premium does the opposite.

Elon sits on both sides of that table. That is the conflict everyone keeps dancing around.

There is also the China problem. 

Tesla manufactures there. And SpaceXAI is a U.S. national security contractor. Partnerships can live with that tension, but a full legal combination of the two companies has to resolve it.

And here is the thing a lot of merger-or-bust commentary skips: a lot of the synergy is already happening without a merger. 

Terafab. Starlink in Tesla vehicles. Megapacks at SpaceX sites. Grok. Shared talent. Shared chips. Shared AI story. You do not need to have one ticker to get most of that.

I still think a combination of the two companies is more likely than not over a longer time window. Think years, not months. I also still think such an announcement, if it comes, is more constructive for $TSLA stock price in the short run than for $SPCX, because a bid has to be competitive and Elon has reasons to want Tesla priced higher, not lower.

That does not mean $SPCX is the weaker company. But the promise of the premise still has to ramp. Price can still test lower while that happens. I have been watching the 4-hour MA75 and the Gann work on $SPCX for that reason. As a technical price analyst, I look at levels first and narrative second.

I can tell you I believe SpaceXAI will accomplish every one of its goals due the incredible resilience of their execution teams. But even if we all believe it together, that won’t change the price discovery process.

If you are waiting for merger clarity before you decide what you own, you may be waiting through the best part of the ranges both stocks are building right now.

Clarity would remove one source of noise. It would not automatically re-rate either stock. $TSLA still has to show the auto business can fund the AI business. $SPCX still has to digest float, spend, and Starship. 

A deal doesn’t erase those tasks. It just puts them onto one balance sheet.

The market today is trying to do two things at once. It is pricing a possible deal it cannot underwrite yet, and it is pricing two very expensive standalone businesses that are still spending their way into the next chapter.

Expect price volatility to continue, and watch the most critical price levels. 

As my friend The @GreatMattsby always says: 

“Be bullish at support and cautious at resistance.”

Not financial advice, but I personally will keep adding new money to my positions in both stocks, steadily over time. 

No matter what price does in the short term, I believe both stock charts will continue to go up and to the right in the long term.

Near $500 for $TSLA (late 2025)

The stock printed a split-adjusted high of $498.83 and a record close of $489.88 in mid-December 2025, a $1.6–1.7T company. 

The financials underneath that price were not a boom. 

They were a mature auto franchise that had already rolled over, with energy and services papering over the hole, and cash still coming in because Tesla had not yet opened the capex floodgates.

Volume was the tell. Full-year 2025 deliveries were 1.64 million, down 9% — Tesla’s first annual unit decline. 

Q4 was worse: 418k deliveries, down 16%. Auto revenue fell 10% for the year to $69.5B and 11% in Q4 to $17.7 Billion.

That was demand, mix, pricing, and a nasty calendar effect (Q3 pulled sales ahead of expiring U.S. EV credits; Q4 paid for it). 

Regulatory credits were still material  $542M in Q4, about $2B for the year which meant reported auto profit was not “pure car economics.”

The rest of the P&L was the offset. Energy grew 27% to $12.8B with record storage deployments (46.7 GWh for the year, 14.2 GWh in Q4). 

Services grew 19% to $12.5 Billion. 

Those two lines are why total revenue only fell 3% to $94.8B even though the car business shrank. 

Mix and cost work also showed up late: Q4 gross margin jumped to 20.1%, auto gross margin recovered into the high teens, and Q4 operating margin was 5.7%. 

For the full year, though, the story was compression: operating income $4.4B (-38%), operating margin 4.6% (from 7.2% in 2024 and 16.8% in 2022), GAAP net income $3.8B (-46%), diluted EPS $1.08.

Cash was the part bulls could still point to without squinting. 

Capex was held to $8.5B (down vs 2024). 

Operating cash flow stayed huge at $14.7 Billion. 

Free cash flow was $6.2B, up 74%. Cash and investments ended at $44.1 Billion. 

Opex was rising, R&D and SG&A were climbing as Tesla leaned into AI and FSD but it had not yet overpowered a still-positive cash machine. 

Q4 FCF was still +$1.4B.

So the $500 bid was not “look at these earnings.” Trailing P/E was already 300x on $3.8B of profit. 

The market was paying a clean option premium: robotaxi, unsupervised FSD, Optimus, energy scale stacked on a company that was still generating several billion of free cash and had not yet forced investors to fund the buildout out of current earnings. 

Fundamentally, it was a weaker auto year with a stronger cash year, priced as if the next act would not cost the current act.

I think what’s happening in Austin right now is going to change how Wall Street looks at $TSLA. 

Since September 3, people in Austin have been paying for rides in Tesla Cybercabs with no steering wheel, no pedals, and no human driver. Then on October 10, Tesla announced that more than 300 Cybercabs are now serving Austin, an 8x increase in just 30 days. Then, right after, Tesla’s head of AI software, Ashok Elluswamy, said Dallas is coming soon.

Just 2 yrs ago, the Cybercab was something we saw on a stage. I remember so many people thought it would never happen. And today, real customers are getting picked up, going about their day, and paying Tesla for the ride. This is now a real service operating on public roads.

I’ve experienced Cybercab myself, and I think people are underestimating just how big this is about to become.

You see, when Tesla sells a car, it collects $ money from that sale. On the other hand, when Tesla operates a Cybercab, that same vehicle can keep generating revenue, ride after ride, day after day, potentially for the life of the car.

This is a COMPLETELY different business that Tesla just opened up. 

And this is something incredibly valuable that is very difficult for most companies to build from scratch. Tesla already manufactures hundreds of thousands of vehicles every quarter, develops its own self-driving software, and has a massive fleet of 10M+ customer vehicles providing real-world driving experience.

Now imagine that manufacturing scale being used to produce vehicles that both 1/ get sold to customers, AND 2/ continue earning $ money for Tesla throughout their working lives.

Of course, putting 300 Cybercabs on the road is not the same as proving a profitable business… we still need to see what each vehicle earns, how much it costs to operate, how safely and reliably it performs, and how quickly Tesla can expand it. 

But this is exactly why Austin matters so much… it’s where Tesla starts turning years of promises into actual business results.

And once Tesla can show that a Cybercab makes $ money consistently, and that the business can grow from hundreds of vehicles to thousands and eventually tens of thousands, it’s really hard for me to see how Wall Street can keep looking at Tesla through the same lens as a traditional car company.

You have to start valuing Tesla as a growing transportation network that can generate revenue every time someone needs a ride.

Tesla's fleet generates real-world data, X and Grok have additional data and SpaceX has its own data. Currently Tesla and SpaceX data are separate and have corporate boundaries and conflict disclosure issues

$TSLA just released its new Robotaxi Safety Report and the numbers are pretty incredible.

According to Tesla, its Robotaxi fleet has now driven over 3.3M miles autonomously, with zero reported injuries counted under its methodology, ZERO airbag deployments in its vehicles, and zero pedestrians or cyclists hit. To put that into perspective, Tesla estimates that human drivers covering the same distance under comparable conditions would have been involved in approximately 9.1 injury collisions, 4.1 collisions involving airbag deployments, and 0.52 collisions involving pedestrians or cyclists.

What's particularly interesting here is that Tesla is finally giving investors a dedicated way to track the safety performance of its Robotaxi fleet, rather than simply relying on demonstrations or statements from Elon Musk. And this is extremely important because safety is arguably one of the biggest hurdles Tesla needs to overcome before Robotaxis can scale nationwide. Regulators, insurers, and consumers all need evidence that autonomous vehicles can operate safely without someone behind the wheel.

Now, keep in mind that these figures cover a specific subset of Tesla's operations without onboard safety monitors, and 3.3 million miles is still a relatively small sample when we're talking about proving long-term safety across different driving conditions. But if Tesla can maintain these results as its fleet expands into more cities and accumulates tens or eventually hundreds of millions of miles, the implications could be enormous for the broader autonomous driving industry.

For $TSLA shareholders, this is exactly the kind of progress we want to see and the next challenge is proving these safety results can hold up at a much larger scale.

Did you know that beating Uber, Lyft and Waymo is too small a goal for Tesla? And one number shows why 🔥

$TSLA’s Robotaxi is growing fast. Cybercabs have been giving paid rides in Austin since September, Dallas follows next month, and unsupervised miles grew eightfold last quarter.

So naturally, most people judge Tesla against those three rivals. The debate is usually about who has more cars, cheaper fares and more cities.

That’s the wrong scoreboard! The better question is how many miles Americans travel by car each year, and how many of those miles happen in a ride-hailing car at all.

The answer is surprisingly lopsided. For every mile Americans ride in an Uber, Lyft, Waymo or any other ride-hailing car, they drive about 70 miles in their own.

That’s the number that matters: 70 🔥

Picture all the miles Americans travel by car as a pizza cut into 71 slices. Ride-hailing gets one slice. The other 70 are driven by people behind the wheel of their own cars.

So the market Uber, Lyft and Waymo fight over is only a little over 1 percent of American driving. The real prize is everything else, and that's the market Tesla is going after.

Once you see that, a lot of Tesla's choices suddenly make sense: the 30-cents-per-mile target, the giant Cybercab production plans, and Elon's claim that Tesla will end up carrying most of the world's passenger miles.

🧮 WHERE THE 70 COMES FROM

America's cars, SUVs and pickups covered about 2.9 trillion miles in 2023, according to the Federal Highway Administration. That's 259 million vehicles averaging about 11,100 miles each.

A 70x gap puts ride-hailing at roughly 40 billion miles a year. Uber and Lyft's own commissioned study fits that scale. Even in six major metro areas where both services are popular, including San Francisco and Boston, the two companies made up just 1 to 3 percent of all miles driven. In other words, even in its strongest cities, ride-hailing only gets one or two slices of the pizza.

Ride-hailing changed how we get to the airport. It barely touched how America actually gets around.

💸 WHY RIDE-HAILING ONLY GETS ONE SLICE

The reason is price. A typical 5-mile UberX ride costs about $15 to $22 in most US cities this year. With fees included, that works out to roughly $3 to $4.40 per mile.

AAA's 2026 study puts the full cost of owning a new car at about 86 cents per mile. That figure counts depreciation, financing, fuel and maintenance.

When riding costs three to five times more than owning, people buy cars. They save ride-hailing for the airport, the bar and the occasional emergency. A big share of every fare pays the human behind the wheel, and that cost doesn't shrink with scale.

⚡ HOW 30 CENTS UNLOCKS THE OTHER 70

Tesla's target for its Robotaxi fleet is 30 cents per mile. On last week's Q3 call, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said Tesla isn't there yet but sees a clear path as the fleet scales.

The trick isn't only removing the driver. The average American car drives about 30 miles a day and sits parked the rest of the time. A robotaxi working most of the day could plausibly cover 250 miles or more. That spreads the cost of one vehicle over eight or nine times as many miles, and that is how the price per mile collapses.

At 30 cents, riding becomes cheaper than owning, even with a healthy margin on top. That's when the other 70 slices finally come within reach.

This isn't about replacing the Tesla already in your garage, since each extra mile in a car you own costs very little. Elon said on the call that the Model 3, Model Y and Roadster remain the cars people will want to own, while Cybercab is mostly Tesla-owned transport-as-a-service. The real fight is over the next car someone decides whether to buy, especially the second one.

🏭 ONE SLICE VS. 70 SLICES

This is where the number gets wild. Suppose each robotaxi covers about 100,000 miles a year. Then the one slice ride-hailing serves today would need only around 400,000 vehicles.

On the Q3 call, Tesla said its Cybercab line in Texas has a listed capacity of more than 125,000 a year, and Lars Moravy added that the line can actually do significantly more. Even at the listed rate, that single line could build enough cars to cover all of today's US ride-hailing in about three years.

The other 70 slices would take closer to 29 million vehicles. At that same rate, one line would need more than two centuries to get there. Tesla's factory ambitions only make sense against that bigger market. Building a Cybercab line just to fight Uber would be like building a stadium for a dinner party.

🔮 THE REAL TARGET

On the call, Elon said Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth wherever it's allowed to operate freely.

Read next to the 70x gap, that isn't a ride-hailing prediction. Ride-hailing holds just one slice out of 71, so a majority can only come from the miles people drive themselves today.

For a century, owning a car has been the cheapest way to get door to door on your own schedule. At 30 cents a mile, that would no longer be true 🔥

If you ask the Tesla engineers behind Cybercab to sum up its design in one rule, the answer is these four plain words: "donot waste a gram" 🔥

It sounds like a simple rule about using less. But the closer you look, the smarter it gets 🔥

✂️ WHAT $TSLA DELETED

Model 3 and Model Y surround their battery electronics with a separate wall, top cover, seal, and a handful of bolts. Cybercab replaces all of that with a single stamping, and that same battery cover doubles as the car's floor.

The heat pump's compressor bolts straight onto the refrigerant manifold, wiping out every refrigerant hose in the system. And instead of running dedicated high-voltage circuits from the battery to the thermal system, Cybercab simply taps power from the drive inverter, which already carries high voltage.

The electric oil pump is gone, along with its circuitry and firmware, replaced by a simple mechanical one. So is the one-shot pyro fuse. The front and rear body modules even skip e-coating, part of eliminating a paint shop that can cost a few hundred million dollars to build.

Even fun gets audited. Tesla's head of drive units isn't a fan of Easter eggs, because someone would have to spend time grinding a logo into a die that never needed one. As a colleague put it, if it adds a penny, it's too much.

⚖️ SPENDING A LITTLE TO SAVE A LOT

Here's the twist. Sometimes not wasting a gram means adding one.

Every battery module board now gets a wireless chip, adding 20 to 30 cents to its cost. In exchange, Tesla deletes a communications harness that might cost about a dollar, plus roughly 50 cents to install. Robots hate harnesses too, because they're notoriously messy to automate.

The battery enclosure switches to steel, which costs about $1.90 per kilogram versus $5 to $8 for aluminum. To get it down to just 1.2 millimeters thick, engineers add local reinforcements and extra parts exactly where they're needed. Steel loses on weight, but Tesla says the numbers still come out ahead on cost.

The motor's cooling passages move out of pricey electrical steel and into the cheaper die-cast aluminum surrounding it. Every job goes to the cheapest material that can do it well.

🏋️ THE WAR ON HIDDEN PADDING

Padding is one of the sneakiest ways a car gains weight. If the target is 1,600 kilograms, every team designs to 1,600. The car still has to meet every requirement, but no team gets to slip in its own 20% cushion on top.

Testing works the same way. Parts are expected to fail between 95% and 100% of their spec, because a part that survives far beyond it is hauling around material it doesn't need.

That matters because weight snowballs. A heavier car needs bigger brakes and a stronger structure, which pile on even more weight.

The good news is that efficiency snowballs too. Cybercab turned out more efficient than Tesla expected, so the pack needed fewer cells than planned, leaving spare room inside.

♻️ WASTE IS MEASURED OVER A LIFETIME

The rule doesn't stop at the factory door.

Battery modules are now potted individually instead of as one solid pack. If one module fails, three healthy ones worth about $1,500 each get saved. On a Model Y structural pack, that same failure means replacing the whole thing.

Reusable contactors can cut power under load a few times and keep right on working, so a minor fender bender doesn't have to blow a one-shot fuse and send the car to service.

We usually judge a car's efficiency the day it rolls out of the factory. Tesla is judging Cybercab on the day it finally retires, at least half a million miles later, and counting every gram it never had to replace.

To me, it’s still undervalued… I believe the majority of Tesla’s long-term value will come from Cybercab and the Robotaxi network, and we’re still early in seeing what that business can become.

The part I keep coming back to is what each vehicle could earn over its lifetime. A Cybercab in Tesla’s fleet can bring in $ money every time someone takes a ride, day after day, for years. If Tesla can keep those vehicles busy and get the costs low enough, the profit from those rides could eventually be worth far more than the profit from selling the car.

We’re already seeing the first steps too. 

Tesla started Cybercab rides in Austin on September 3. By the end of Q3, its Robotaxi fleet had reached nearly 2 million cumulative unsupervised miles, 8x the total at the end of Q2.

That’s real progress. 

Tesla also builds the vehicles, develops the driving software and operates its own charging network. I think having those pieces together gives it a strong foundation to build on as the service grows. 

Tesla still has to expand safely, get the approvals it needs and make $ money after paying for the vehicles, charging, cleaning, insurance and maintenance, etc. 

Revenue only gets you so far if the costs eat it all up…

That’s why I’m looking years ahead of a lot of people. I want to see how many people use the service, how often each car is working and how much profit the fleet can produce as it grows. My view is that today’s valuation still extremely underestimates what that part of the business could eventually earn.

And also when they allow Tesla owner fleets to be on the Robotaxi network… that’s checkmate. 

As more people experience it in their own cities and Tesla shows what it can earn from those rides, I believe it’ll become obvious to the world why I see $TSLA as undervalued today.
